analysis.one_liner: Lets House candidates run on public campaign funds if they forgo private money, and bans party soft money.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote: after referral to three committees and two subcommittees in May 2001, no further action was taken before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any House candidate qualify for full public campaign financing by collecting 1,500 small $5 contributions from voters and agreeing to reject all other private donations. It would also ban 'soft money' — unlimited contributions to national political parties — require broadcasters to give qualified candidates free airtime at deep discounts, tighten disclosure of campaign ads, cap members' use of taxpayer-funded mass mailings during election season, and strengthen the Federal Election Commission. It died in committee without ever coming to the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates without personal wealth or access to wealthy donors, since qualifying requires only small $5 contributions from voters plus limited $100 'seed money.' Ordinary citizens gain a public alternative to a system where large donors have outsized influence, and taxpayers gain the potential savings the bill's findings cite from legislation shaped by contributor access. Incumbents also gain a way out of constant fundraising, and broadcasters' audiences get more candidate airtime during campaigns.

how_it_helps.text: A candidate who collects 1,500 $5 qualifying contributions and agrees to take no private money receives a public grant sized to recent winning-candidate spending, plus seed money of up to $35,000 in small increments [S3].

If a privately funded opponent or outside group outspends a clean-money candidate beyond 125% of the public grant, the candidate receives matching public funds, capped at 200% of the base amount [S3].

The bill bans national party committees from soliciting or spending soft money and blocks party committees from funneling money to tax-exempt organizations, closing a major channel for unlimited political money [S2] [S3].
Clean money candidates are entitled to free broadcast time in prime hours and ad rates up to 50% below the lowest standard rate [S3].
The bill mandates electronic FEC filing, 24-hour reporting of late contributions, random audits, injunction authority, and a restructured commission to speed up enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through appropriations to a new House of Representatives Election Fund ('such sums as are necessary') [S3]. Broadcasters, who must provide free airtime and sell candidate ads at up to half their lowest rate. Political party committees and large donors, who lose the soft-money channel and face new limits and certifications on party spending. Incumbent members, who lose most franked mass mailings during election season.

drawbacks.text: Public financing is funded by mandatory federal appropriations with no spending cap ('such sums as are necessary'), so taxpayers bear the direct cost of every publicly funded campaign [S3].

Because participation is voluntary, a privately funded candidate can still outspend a clean money opponent; the matching-fund response is capped at 200% of the public grant, so very large private or outside spending could still dominate a race [S3].

The free-airtime mandate and rate discounts impose uncompensated costs on broadcasters and their other advertisers, and such content requirements raised First Amendment concerns about forcing broadcasters to carry candidate speech.

The bill raises some contribution limits as an offset — $30,000 aggregate annual individual giving and $10,000 to state party committees — which its critics could call a loosening of the rules elsewhere [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core promise — a real option to run for the House without private fundraising — is substantive and directly aimed at reducing the influence of large contributors. The honest costs are real: open-ended taxpayer funding of campaigns, uncompensated burdens on broadcasters, and the leakage problem that a voluntary system cannot stop unlimited spending by candidates and outside groups who opt out. Its public-matching mechanism and soft-money ban are broad and aggressive, making it a far larger intervention than the narrower law Congress actually passed the following year, and its free-airtime mandate would have faced serious court challenges.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and split between two subcommittees in May 2001, and nothing more ever happened to it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the Clean Money, Clean Elections Act on April 26, 2001, joined at introduction by 49 other members [S3].
It gathered 51 cosponsors — 50 of the chamber's Democrats and its one Independent [S4] [S1].
The Speaker referred it to the House Administration, Energy and Commerce, and Government Reform committees on the day of introduction [S5].
In early May 2001 it was sent to the Government Efficiency subcommittee and the Telecommunications and Internet subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded afterward [S5].
The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003 with the bill still in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbents and party committees who rely on soft money and large private contributions, and broadcasters, all kept the existing system intact; no challenger's fundraising burden was lifted.

sides.party_line_note: All 51 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican sponsored it, and the three Republican chairmen who controlled its committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill mandates free prime-time airtime for clean money candidates, caps candidate ad rates at 50% of the lowest standard rate, and bars preempting paid candidate ads — costs the networks and stations would absorb without compensation.

industries.industry: Political parties (national, state, and local committees)
industries.note: The bill bans party soft money, prohibits donations to tax-exempt groups, caps party spending in races with a clean money candidate, and requires party committees to certify they will not mix coordinated and independent spending.

Clean money candidates cannot accept private contributions beyond small seed money ($100 per person, $35,000 total), and incumbents lose most franked mass mailings during campaign season — removing major advantages of money in House races.
Party committees would be barred from soliciting funds for 501(c) organizations, and 'issue advertisements' naming candidates would face new disclosure requirements within 48 hours.
